title: What our people are telling us
source: Your Voice survey (responses to 21 October); analysis 30 October 2026.
notes: [0:00 – 0:30] Good morning. We analysed the Your Voice survey: 327 people, 30 questions and almost 1,900 written comments. In the next 20 minutes we will tell you what employees value, what they want fixed first, and a simple 90-day plan to start.

title: Three things to remember
notes: [0:30 – 1:30] Here is the whole story in one slide. One: people are proud of this company and they help each other. That is a real strength. Two: they want people decisions, like promotions, pay rises and recognition, to be fair and clear. These are the lowest scores in the survey. Three: they want leaders to listen and then act. It was the number one thing people asked HR to do better. Our plan is one 90-day pilot, starting in Customer Service.

title: Who took part
notes: [1:30 – 2:30] 327 people answered. They could reply in English, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil or Malayalam, from 23 locations, and they wrote almost 1,900 comments. Mumbai is the biggest group, about 40% of answers, and 38% have been here less than 3 years. One limit: we were not given the total number of employees, so we cannot say what share of staff took part.

title:
The good news: people are proud
and they help each other
notes: [3:00 – 4:00] Let's start with the good news, because it is big. Almost everyone understands how their work helps the business. 92% are proud to work here. 91% say people in their team help each other, and 90% feel they belong. When we asked what people never want to lose, 119 people named their team or colleagues. Whatever we change, we must protect this.

title:
One warning: answers with a name
look more positive
notes: [4:00 – 5:30] One important warning. The survey asked people for their name, and 69% gave it. People who stayed anonymous were clearly less positive. For example, 92% of named people plan to stay 3 to 5 years, but only 78% of anonymous people. People may be more careful when their name is attached. So the real picture is probably a little less rosy than the headline numbers. Our simple advice: do not ask for names next time.

title: How we decided what to fix first
source: Notebook Step 7.3; pass marks fixed before reading the result.
notes: [6:30 – 8:00] Low scores alone are not enough to choose priorities, so we checked every theme in four ways. One: is the score low? Two: does it move together with people wanting to stay and recommend the company? Three: did people pick it when asked what HR should do better? Four: did people raise it on their own when we asked for one change? We set the pass marks before looking at the results.

title: Two themes pass all four tests
notes: [8:00 – 9:00] Here is the result. Only two themes are strong on all four tests: fair people decisions with career growth, and leaders who listen and act. Those are our two priorities. Recognition scores lowest and people write about it a lot, so we put it inside priority one. Teamwork across teams is real but smaller, so it gets a targeted fix. Pay and facilities matter to people but there was no survey question on them, so we send them to the yearly review.

title:
Priority 1: fair decisions
that people understand
source: item_evidence_profile.csv; driver_model_summary.csv; hr_priority_counts.csv; quote verbatim, de-identified.
notes: [9:00 – 10:30] Priority one is fair decisions that people understand. Only 75% say people decisions are made consistently. Of the areas leaders can change, fairness is the one most linked to people wanting to stay and recommend the company. And 51 people said HR's main job should be helping careers grow. In one employee's words: inconsistent performance evaluations and opaque promotion criteria. What it means in practice: clear rules for promotion, pay and rewards, and a reason given for every decision.

title:
Priority 2: leaders who listen,
and then act
notes: [10:30 – 12:00] Priority two is leaders who listen and then act. We asked everyone to pick the one thing HR should do better. The top answer, by a clear margin, was listening to employees and their concerns: 67 people. Today only 80% say leaders act on feedback, and among the actionable questions it is the one most linked to people wanting to stay. People are not asking for more announcements. They want proof that when they raise something, something happens.

title: Where to start: Customer Service
notes: [12:00 – 13:00] Where should we start? This table shows the share of positive answers by group, and darker means lower. Customer Service is the lowest group on almost everything: only 57% feel recognised, and 76% plan to stay. People with 3 to 5 years' service also dip. Women answer less positively than men on fairness and recognition. This is not about blaming a team. It tells us where to listen first and where a pilot can make the biggest difference.

title: A smaller fix: handovers between teams
notes: [13:00 – 14:00] There is one smaller issue. People rate their own team very highly, 91%, but teams working together across the company lower, 82%. 45 people rate their own team well but other teams poorly. It is real, but smaller than the two priorities, and people rarely raised it on their own. So we suggest a targeted fix: take one handover in Customer Service and agree who sends what, who receives it, and who covers when someone is away.

title: What else people told us
notes: [14:00 – 15:00] When we asked an open question, if you could make one change, people mostly asked for better communication, recognition, career growth and follow-through. That matches our two priorities. People also care about pay, benefits and facilities: 51 people picked it as HR's main job. A 90-day pilot cannot fix pay, so we suggest sending it to the yearly pay and facilities review, and telling people clearly that this is where it went.

title:
Our plan: one 90-day pilot,
three parts
source: implementation_roadmap_0_90_days.csv (revised IDs P1, P2, T); proposed owners, not approved commitments.
notes: [15:00 – 16:30] Here is the plan. One 90-day pilot with three parts, starting in Customer Service. Part one, owned by the HR head: publish clear rules for promotion, pay and rewards, give a reason for every decision, and have managers recognise each person every month. Part two, owned by a leadership sponsor: log every concern with an owner and a date, and send a monthly 'you said, we did' update. Part three, owned by the Operations head: fix one handover between teams. None of this needs a new system.

title: 90 days, step by step
notes: [16:30 – 17:30] Step by step. In the first two weeks we choose the pilot teams, check today's rules and run a short anonymous survey as our starting point. By day 30 the rules are published, owners are named and the concern log is open. From day 31 to 60 we run it, review problems every week and check it is not adding paperwork. In the last month we repeat the short survey and decide together: grow it, change it or stop it.

title: How we will know it worked
source: roadmap_kpi_dictionary.csv; item_evidence_profile.csv. Targets are suggestions to confirm in the first 14 days.
notes: [17:30 – 18:30] How will we know it worked? For each part we check two things: did we do the work, and did employees notice? For example, rules published for every pilot role, and the share who say decisions are consistent going up from 75% by about 5 points. We measure with a short anonymous survey so people can be honest. And we watch our strengths, pride and teamwork, to make sure they do not drop.
